title: GM Smart Driver — the cars that told insurers how you brake
hooks: Your GM car may have reported your hard braking to insurers.
Every hard stop in millions of GM cars was allegedly for sale.
A safe-driving feature allegedly raised some drivers' insurance.
GM just paid 220 million dollars over how you brake.
Over 370,000 drivers were told they weren't tracked. They were.

scenes.narration: [serious] Your GM car may have reported your hard braking to insurers. Now it cost GM 220 million dollars.
From 2016 to 2024, GM ran Smart Driver. It promised safer driving.
Most joined at the dealership, alongside OnStar. States say staff sometimes clicked yes for them.
So what did it record? Every trip. Hard braking, fast starts, speeding.
The twist? States allege GM sold it to brokers, then insurers. Some premiums went up.
GM's app told over 370,000 drivers they weren't enrolled. They were.
On October 29, 36 attorneys general settled. As one said, people bought a car, not a tracking device.

facts.claim: GM agreed on Oct 29, 2026 to pay $220 million to settle claims by 36 attorneys general (35 states + DC), led by Oregon and Washington
Smart Driver ran from 2016 to 2024, enrolled millions of drivers, was marketed as improving driving safety; GM says it ended the product in 2024
Most customers enrolled at dealerships in a single sign-up that also covered OnStar; staff allegedly accepted terms on customers' behalf; sales staff got bonuses partly based on enrollments
Data collected: number of trips, start and end time of each drive, hard braking and rapid acceleration counts, whether the driver exceeded the speed limit
GM allegedly sold driving and location data to data brokers who sold it to insurers, which used it partly to set rates and sometimes raised premiums
The OnStar app wrongly told over 370,000 drivers they weren't enrolled; GM later unenrolled them without disclosing the error
Settlement requires GM to get affirmative express consent before collecting or sharing driving and location data
Oregon AG Dan Rayfield: 'People bought a car, not a tracking device.'
Separate FTC order (finalized Jan 2026) bans GM/OnStar from sharing such data with consumer reporting agencies for five years; NYT reported data went to LexisNexis and Verisk

seo.title: GM Pays $220 Million Over Selling Drivers' Braking Data to Insurers
seo.description: On October 29, 2026, General Motors agreed to pay $220 million to 36 attorneys general over its Smart Driver program. States allege GM sold trip, hard-braking and speeding data to brokers who sold it to insurers, without drivers' consent. GM ended Smart Driver in 2024 and must now get consent first. #privacy #gm #shorts
